task.goal: Write the life this cycle's record produced. Lead with a named interviewed person or a Packet-named place. The feed or tracker line is the weather, never the lede.
task.assignment: Voices, 2026-10-22: Marcus Webb in their own words, and 3 more
task.approach: Voices approach: this slice is what citizens wrote on their own pages — verbatim, attributed, the day it happened. The person's own line first, before their name; then who they are in one plain clause; then what in the city they were answering, from the page's own tags. Fewer, longer passages; the words are the product. Never a count, never a statistic, never an explanation of what they meant. Facts on this slice: the names, places, roles and numbers listed. Those are real; do not invent people or places. Everything else about this beat — what it looks like, who is there, what they want and hate — is yours to paint.

facts: “Month eleven’s done, $400K moved, and the queue’s finally down to six files waiting on title search. I keep telling myself twenty-three days is fine, it’s the standard, but the standard doesn’t tell me which of those six households is one missed payment from losing it all. I walked past a couple of the addresses on my way home—didn’t stop, just saw the lights on, and that’s the whole game, isn’t it. The spreadsheet says we’re ahead, but the spreadsheet never has to sit in a kitchen and explain a delay. Tomorrow I’ll push the title vendor again, and tonight I’ll just let the numbers sit.” — Marcus Webb, OEWD Program Director, Downtown (own page, after work, C112)

“The Chinatown call still sits heavy. We got someone there eventually, but the wait was too long, and I know West Oakland’s crews would’ve been faster. That’s the part nobody puts in the report—the minutes that stretch when you’re waiting and the system already knows better. I keep pushing the district-level data because I need the city to see the gap the way I do, not as a line on a spreadsheet but as a block where someone’s neighbor could’ve been the one answering. I’m tired of being the one who knows what’s possible and still has to argue for it.” — Vanessa Tran-Muñoz, OARI Program Director, Rockridge (own page, after work, C112)

“The Fruitvale number keeps coming back. Eighteen percent on my internal sheet, twenty-three on the public file—someone's rounding, or someone's lag. I don't know which bothers me more. Federal habit: I want to build the case myself, drive the interview, but that's not this job now. I'm managing gaps I can't close, just watching where the protocol catches and where it doesn't. West Oakland tonight, same as every night. I should eat something.” — Clarissa Dane, DISTRICT ATTORNEY, West Oakland (own page, after work, C112)

“Yu Zen’s file is still open on my desk. Twenty-nine years old, Rockridge, and now he’s looking at months of rehab for a hand that might never close right. Deacon’s losing his, I know that much already. Some days I wonder if the board sees the numbers or the people behind them, and I’m too tired to keep fighting that fight tonight. I just keep coming back to the same question: did we get there fast enough, and will it ever feel like we did?” — Priya Narang, EMS DIRECTOR, Uptown (own page, after work, C112)

I want to know that we're processing these applications fast enough to make a difference in people's lives. I'm pushing for faster processing because every delay feels like we're risking someone falling through the cracks.

sources.name: Vanessa Tran-Muñoz
sources.quote: The Voices page for this cycle creates accountability for me because it shows the real human impact of our work. Marcus Webb's words, for example, are a reminder that we're not just processing numbers, we're affecting people's lives. What I want is for the city to see the gaps in our response times and understand that it's not just about statistics, it's about people's experiences. I want the city to recognize that trained neighbors can make a difference, just like we proved in West Oakland.

sources.name: Clarissa Dane
sources.quote: As DISTRICT ATTORNEY, I've seen firsthand how the city's data management affects our community. The OARI protocols look good on paper, but I'm still waiting to see them hold up when things get tough. I'm pushing for better district-level data because I need the city to understand the gaps we're facing here in West Oakland. It's not just about numbers; it's about people and response times that can make all the difference.

sources.name: Priya Narang
sources.quote: The Voices page for this cycle makes me think about accountability because it has my own words on it, and people like Marcus Webb's. Seeing my own reflection on the page alongside others makes me accountable. I want to be able to say that we've done better by the people we're supposed to help. I want to be able to look at cases like Yu Zen's and know we did everything we could.

approvedQuotes.text: The Voices page for this cycle keeps me accountable because it shows the real people behind the numbers. I'm still thinking about the Johnson application, where one missing document is holding up an entire family's assistance. I want to know that we're processing these applications fast enough to make a difference in people's lives. I'm pushing for faster processing because every delay feels like we're risking someone falling through the cracks.

The Voices page for this cycle creates accountability for me because it shows the real human impact of our work. Marcus Webb's words, for example, are a reminder that we're not just processing numbers, we're affecting people's lives. What I want is for the city to see the gaps in our response times and understand that it's not just about statistics, it's about people's experiences. I want the city to recognize that trained neighbors can make a difference, just like we proved in West Oakland.

As DISTRICT ATTORNEY, I've seen firsthand how the city's data management affects our community. The OARI protocols look good on paper, but I'm still waiting to see them hold up when things get tough. I'm pushing for better district-level data because I need the city to understand the gaps we're facing here in West Oakland. It's not just about numbers; it's about people and response times that can make all the difference.

The Voices page for this cycle makes me think about accountability because it has my own words on it, and people like Marcus Webb's. Seeing my own reflection on the page alongside others makes me accountable. I want to be able to say that we've done better by the people we're supposed to help. I want to be able to look at cases like Yu Zen's and know we did everything we could.
